charts.title: Liquidity Risk
charts.sub: How tight US money conditions are, as a percentile of their own history (0 loose, 1 very tight)
charts.desc: Risk assets (stocks and crypto) tend to do best when money is loose and worst when it is tight. This score blends the 10-year real yield, the US dollar, credit spreads, money-supply (M2) growth and the Fed's net liquidity (balance sheet minus Treasury cash and reverse repos). High score = tight conditions, which are less supportive for risk assets.
charts.how: Five inputs from FRED, each turned into its own percentile (past only), averaged, then smoothed over 3 months. Needs at least 3 inputs available. Net liquidity growth uses WALCL minus TGA minus reverse repo.

charts.title: Credit Spread Risk
charts.sub: Moody's Baa corporate yield minus the 10-year Treasury, as a percentile of its own history
charts.desc: How much extra yield investors demand to hold risky company debt instead of government bonds. When that gap widens fast, lenders are getting nervous and credit is tightening, which has come before most recessions and many equity and crypto drawdowns. High score = spreads wide for their own history.
charts.how: Source: FRED BAA10Y (monthly average). Score = where the latest spread sits among every spread seen up to that month (0 = tightest ever, 1 = widest ever). No look-ahead.

charts.title: Yield Curve Recession Risk
charts.sub: US 10-year minus 3-month Treasury yield; the more inverted it is, the higher the score
charts.desc: When short-term rates rise above long-term rates (an inverted curve) it has signalled a US recession ahead in every downturn since the 1970s, usually 6 to 18 months early. High score = curve inverted or very flat compared with its history.
charts.how: Source: FRED T10Y3M (monthly average). Score = 1 / (1 + e^(2.2 × (spread + 0.3))): about 0.5 when the curve is slightly inverted (-0.3 points), above 0.8 when clearly inverted (-1 point), near 0.1 when it is a healthy +0.7. A warning gauge, not a timing tool.

charts.title: Employment Recession Risk
charts.sub: The Sahm rule gauge: how far US unemployment has risen above its recent low
charts.desc: Rising unemployment is one of the most reliable signs that a recession has started. The Sahm rule fires when the 3-month average unemployment rate is 0.5 points above its lowest level of the past year; it has flagged every US recession since 1970. High score = unemployment is climbing fast.
charts.how: Source: FRED SAHMREALTIME (monthly). Score = 1 / (1 + e^(-6 × (indicator - 0.35))): about 0.1 at 0, 0.5 at 0.35, above 0.7 once the 0.5 rule fires. A confirming gauge: it usually lights up after a recession has begun.

charts.title: Production & Business Recession Risk
charts.sub: Year-on-year change in US industrial production; weak or falling output means higher risk
charts.desc: Factories, mines and utilities react early when demand fades. Industrial production falling year on year has accompanied most US recessions. High score = output is shrinking or growing very slowly.
charts.how: Source: FRED INDPRO (monthly index), year-on-year change. Score = 1 / (1 + e^(1 × (growth + 1))): about 0.27 at 0% growth, 0.5 at -1%, above 0.85 when output is down 3% or more.

charts.title: National Income & Product Recession Risk
charts.sub: US real GDP growth, quarterly (annualised); slow or negative growth means higher risk
charts.desc: GDP is the broadest measure of the economy. Two quarters in a row of falling GDP is the common rule of thumb for a recession. High score = growth is slow or negative. It is published late and revised, so it confirms rather than predicts.
charts.how: Source: FRED A191RL1Q225SBEA (real GDP, % change at annual rate, quarterly). Score = 1 / (1 + e^(1.2 × (growth - 0.5))): about 0.35 at 0%, 0.5 at +0.5%, above 0.9 at -2%.

charts.title: Bitcoin Risk
charts.sub: One 0 to 1 gauge of how stretched Bitcoin is, combining five valuation measures. You can change how much each counts.
charts.desc: Low scores have been where Bitcoin was cheap against its own history; high scores where it was stretched. It says where we are in the cycle, not what happens next. Use the sliders to remove or down-weight any measure and see how the score changes.
charts.how: Five measures, each turned into a percentile of its own past (no look-ahead) and smoothed over 7 days: price vs the 200-week average, price vs the log-regression trend, MVRV, MVRV Z-Score and the Puell Multiple. The score is their weighted average. Starts mid 2014 so there is enough history to rank.

charts.title: Total Market Cap Risk
charts.sub: How stretched the whole crypto market is against its own long-term trend, as a percentile of its history
charts.desc: The same idea as Bitcoin Risk, applied to the total value of all crypto. Low scores have been where the market was cheap against its own history; high scores where it was stretched. It says where we are in the cycle, not what happens next.
charts.how: Two measures, each a percentile of its own past (no look-ahead), smoothed over 7 days: total market cap against its 200-week average and against its log-regression trend. Source: TTM's market history (Coin Metrics and CoinGecko based). Starts mid 2014.

charts.title: Logarithmic Regression
charts.sub: Bitcoin price (weekly, daily for the last 3 years; use the 1y and 2y range buttons to zoom in) with a long-term trend line and bands at ±1 and ±2 standard deviations (fitted on all data since 2011; slope 5.49)
charts.desc: A straight line fitted through Bitcoin's price on log scales shows its long-term growth path. The bands show how far price has historically swung from that path. Price near the bottom band has been cheap and near the top band stretched. Growth has been slowing over time, so older fits overstate the future.
charts.how: Least squares fit of ln(price) against ln(days since the genesis block, 3 Jan 2009), using daily prices from 2011. Bands are the standard deviation of the fit errors. This is fitted with hindsight on purpose: it is a map of the past, not a forecast.

charts.title: Puell Multiple
charts.sub: Daily value of newly mined bitcoin divided by its 365-day average
charts.desc: Miners sell much of what they earn, so the dollar value of new coins is a pulse on miner income. Very low readings (below about 0.5) have lined up with miner capitulation and major cycle lows. Very high readings (above about 4) have lined up with euphoric tops.
charts.how: Daily issuance (block reward from the halving schedule × 144 blocks) × price, divided by its 365-day average. Uses the reward only (not fees), as in the original definition. Halvings: Nov 2012, Jul 2016, May 2020, Apr 2024.

charts.title: VIX Fear (Stocks)
charts.sub: The VIX (expected 30-day S&P 500 volatility), as a percentile of its own history
charts.desc: The VIX shows how much movement options traders expect in the S&P 500 over the next month. It usually moves the opposite way to stocks: it jumps when prices fall fast and sinks when markets drift up calmly. Very high readings (panic) have often sat close to market lows, and very low readings (complacency) often come before sudden shocks. High score = more fear than usual.
charts.how: Source: FRED VIXCLS (daily close, monthly average). Score = where the latest reading sits among every reading seen up to that month (0 = calmest ever, 1 = most fearful ever). No look-ahead.

charts.title: DVOL Fear (Bitcoin)
charts.sub: Deribit's Bitcoin volatility index (crypto's VIX), as a percentile of its own history
charts.desc: DVOL is the Bitcoin version of the VIX. It shows how much price movement Bitcoin options traders expect over the next 30 days. It tends to jump in sell-offs and shrink in quiet, steady trends. Extreme highs have often marked capitulation, while long stretches of very low readings have often come before big moves in either direction. High score = more fear than usual.
charts.how: Source: Deribit public volatility index (daily close, since March 2021). Score = where the latest reading sits among every reading seen up to that day (0 = calmest, 1 = most fearful). It only has about five years of history, so extremes are judged against that window. No look-ahead.
